title: Understanding as foresight, and its limits
claim: In the Book of Wealth அறிவு is repeatedly defined as knowing and guarding against what is coming: 427 makes knowing what will be the mark of the wise, 429 promises them no shaking affliction, and 435 and 535 give the failure two outcomes, sudden ruin and late regret. The book then qualifies this in three directions: the foresight can be obtained through others the ruler keeps (442), understanding also dissolves trouble that has already come (622), and 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish, which Parimelazhagar extends to one who has every understanding. Read together, foresight is the working core of understanding in statecraft, but neither wholly one's own nor proof against fate.
limits: The verses do not say foresight is the whole of அறிவு; elsewhere the term is tested morally (203, 315) and by seeing the real (355). The pull between 372 and 429 belongs with the fate-and-agency conflict and is not resolved in the verses.

title: Does understanding follow the world or test it?
claim: Several verses make accord with the world part of what understanding is: the much-studied who cannot move with the world lack understanding (140), to live as the world lives is அறிவு (426), and even after knowing a method one should act knowing how the world goes (637). 850 extends this from conduct to belief: one who denies what the world affirms is set down as a demon. Yet 423, in the same chapter as 426, defines understanding as finding the true substance of a thing whoever says it. Parimelazhagar narrows 'the world' in 140 and 850 to the high-minded many and reads 426 as advice to a king, and Kalaignar's 'shown by evidence' moves 850 toward 423.
limits: On Parimelazhagar's reading 214 also makes knowing the way of the world the test of being alive, but Manakkudavar takes ஒத்தது there as ஒப்புரவு, so it is weak support. The 850-423 conflict is already noted under knowing_and_learning; this thread concerns the world as a standard, not the speaker's standing.

title: The sulk: love's best part, in measure
claim: The Book of Love keeps returning to ஊடல், and its verses raise and then bound it. 1109 lists sulking with reconciliation and union as love's rewards; 1326 ranks sulking above union, as digestion above eating; 1330, the book's last verse, calls it love's pleasure but places its own pleasure in the embrace that follows. 1302 and 1306 make it a matter of degree, salt that seasons and spoils if prolonged, fruit unripe or overripe without it, and 1282 says that when love is full not a millet-seed of sulking is wanted. Together they treat the sulk as valuable only as a measured step toward union, which Parimelazhagar makes explicit in glossing 1109 and 1330 as ending it at the right point.
limits: The verses come from different speakers and situations (1282 is the woman's impatience voiced as general advice, per Parimelazhagar), so this is a pattern across voices, not one doctrine. Pope's translation of 1109 as lust is a translator's reading.

title: Love measured against liquor
claim: The Book of Love uses liquor, which chapter 93 condemns, as its standard comparison for love, and uses it both ways. In 1090, 1201 and 1281 love surpasses toddy: liquor delights only when drunk, love at a look or a thought, from first sight (1090) through separation (1201) to the woman's longing (1281). In 1145 and 1288 love instead works like drink: wanted more with each exposure, and in 1288 craved though it does shameful harm, which Parimelazhagar spells out as loss of shame, restraint, conduct and awareness, the very charges laid against drink in chapter 93.
limits: The chapter 93 verses are not in this packet; the link to them rests on Parimelazhagar's gloss of 1288. Speakers differ by commentator for 1090, 1145 and 1288, so the thread does not claim a single voice holds both views.
